subtitle: Mothers, Names and Power in the Satavahana Deccan

panels.shot: low-angle wide of rock-cut cave façade with queenly figure in foreground
panels.action: Satavahana Royal Patroness stands at the edge of a monsoon-soaked cliff before a freshly carved rock-cut cave, hand resting on a chisel-bearing artisan, while distant hills fade into rain and mist.

dialogue.text: In the basalt cliffs of the Deccan, kings name themselves after mothers: Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra. What power did these women wield, that stone must remember them?

i18n.hi: दक्कन की बेसाल्ट चट्टानों में, राजा माँ के नाम से जाने जाते हैं: गौतमीपुत्र, वसिष्ठीपुत्र। इन स्त्रियों में कैसी शक्ति थी कि पत्थर भी उन्हें याद रखे?

panels.shot: slow push-in on a bird’s-eye view of the Western Ghats and Godavari valley
panels.action: Rolling green hills of the Western Ghats fall away to the wide Godavari valley, caravan lines threading between towns, while distant rock-cut monasteries cling to dark basalt walls.

dialogue.text: The Deccan in the first centuries of our era is a land of roads and rivers, caravans and caves, where the Satavahana kings hold the plateaus between north and south.

i18n.hi: हमारे युग की पहली सदियों में दक्कन सड़कों–नदियों, कारवाँ–गुफाओं की धरती है, जहाँ सातवाहन उत्तर–दक्षिण के बीच का पठार थामे हैं।

panels.shot: medium close-up on a hand carving letters into rock
panels.action: A calloused hand guides an iron chisel on warm basalt, letters in early Brahmi emerging in neat lines along a cave wall, stone dust clinging to the artisan’s fingers.

dialogue.text: Their history does not survive in court chronicles. It lives in chiselled lines at Nashik, Karla and Kanheri, where donors speak in stone.

i18n.hi: इनकी कहानी दरबारी ग्रंथों में नहीं, नाशिक, कार्ला, कन्हेरी की खुदाई हुई पंक्तियों में बची है, जहाँ दाता खुद पत्थर बन बोलते हैं।

panels.shot: close-up profile of Satavahana Royal Patroness reading an inscription
panels.action: Satavahana Royal Patroness stands in soft cave light, fingers hovering near an inscription, eyes intent, while faint outlines of seated monks appear deeper inside.

dialogue.text: There we first glimpse the royal women: queens, mothers, nuns, merchant wives. Not in gossip, but in their own words, recorded as donors.

i18n.hi: यहीं पहली बार राजमहिलाएँ दिखती हैं: रानियाँ, माताएँ, भिक्षुणियाँ, साहुकार–पत्नी। चुगलियों में नहीं, दान–शिलालेखों में अपने शब्दों से।

panels.shot: medium shot inside a Nashik cave with monks in background
panels.action: Within a cool Nashik cave, Satavahana Royal Patroness gestures toward a stone bench and cistern as robed monks sit quietly in the background, the outside light pooling at the entrance.

dialogue.text: One inscription at Nashik names a royal mother donating a cave and cistern to monks. Her gift is a place to sit, sleep and endure the Deccan heat and rain.

i18n.hi: नाशिक की एक लिखावट में एक राजमाता भिक्षुओं को गुफा और पोखर दान करती है। उसका तोहफा है बैठने, सोने और दक्कन की गर्मी–बरसात सहने की जगह।

panels.shot: low-angle medium of patroness with stylised kingly figure in background silhouette
panels.action: Satavahana Royal Patroness stands firm in the foreground, while behind her a faint, imposing silhouette of a crowned king suggests a son watching from the shadows.

dialogue.text: Yet when her son speaks in stone, he does something unusual for ancient India: he names himself not only as someone’s son, but as the son of his mother.

i18n.hi: पर जब उसका बेटा पत्थर से बोलता है, तो प्राचीन भारत के लिए अनोखी बात करता है: वह खुद को सिर्फ किसी का बेटा नहीं, अपनी माँ का बेटा भी कहता है।

panels.shot: extreme close-up of letters forming ‘Gautamiputrasa’ on rock
panels.action: The carved Brahmi letters curve and angle precisely along the basalt, picking out the word that scholars read as ‘Gautamiputrasa’, edges sharp and deep.

dialogue.text: ‘Gautamiputrasa’ says a line, ‘the son of Gautami’. Elsewhere another king is ‘Vasishthiputrasa’, the son of Vasishthi. The pattern repeats, again and again.

i18n.hi: एक पंक्ति में लिखा है ‘गौतमिपुत्रस’ – गौतमी का बेटा। दूसरी जगह राजा ‘वसिष्ठिपुत्रस’ है – वसिष्ठी का बेटा। यही ढंग बार–बार दोहरता है।

panels.shot: slow push-in on patroness seated in a council hall with men around
panels.action: Satavahana Royal Patroness sits upright in a pillared hall, scrolls and palm-leaf documents before her, while male courtiers and scribes sit respectfully, heads slightly bowed.

dialogue.text: To some modern eyes this looks like a matriarchal court, where mothers rule and trace descent. But the stone is quieter than that. It tells us something smaller, and more precise.

i18n.hi: आज की कुछ आँखों को यह मानो मातृसत्ता लगता है, जैसे माताएँ दरबार चलाती हों। पर पत्थर इससे शांत है; वह हमें कुछ छोटा, पर ज्यादा साफ बताता है।

panels.shot: split-panel style composition showing two queens with different families behind them
panels.action: On one side, a richly dressed queen stands before a clan of brahmana elders; on the other, another queen stands before urban guild leaders, each group distinct in dress and bearing.

dialogue.text: Satavahana kings married more than once. Each mother brought her own lineage: brahmana clans, regional chiefs, merchant houses. A prince’s mother meant a prince’s allies.

i18n.hi: सातवाहन राजाओं की एक से अधिक शादियाँ थीं। हर माँ अपना कुल लाती थी: ब्राह्मण गोत्र, प्रांतीय सरदार, व्यापारी घराने। जिस माँ का बेटा, उसी के साथी उसकी ताकत।

panels.shot: medium shot of patroness placing a hand on a young prince’s shoulder before elders
panels.action: Satavahana Royal Patroness rests a steady hand on a teenage prince’s shoulder before a semi-circle of elders and chiefs, their faces watchful, the air tense with expectation.

dialogue.text: In such a house, a name is a promise. When a king calls himself ‘Gautamiputra’, he publicly ties his throne to his mother’s people. It is alliance, carved as identity.

i18n.hi: ऐसे घर में नाम ही वचन है। जब राजा खुद को ‘गौतमीपुत्र’ कहता है, तो खुलेआम अपना सिंहासन माँ के कुल से बाँध देता है। गठबंधन को ही वह पहचान बनाकर गढ़ता है।

panels.shot: low-angle wide of patroness supervising artisans at Karla cave entrance
panels.action: At the grand façade of a Karla cave, Satavahana Royal Patroness oversees artisans hauling stone and carving pillars, merchants with bales watching from the side, while the forest stretches below.

dialogue.text: And the same women move beyond the palace. At Karla and Kanheri, inscriptions show queens and merchant wives donating halls, pillars, cisterns, even entire villages to monastic communities.

i18n.hi: और ये औरतें महल से आगे बढ़ती हैं। कार्ला, कन्हेरी में शिलालेख दिखाते हैं कि रानियाँ और साहुकार–पत्नियाँ हाल, स्तंभ, पोखर, यहाँ तक कि पूरे गाँव संघों को दान करती हैं।

panels.shot: close-up of patroness handing a small clay seal or token to a monk
panels.action: Satavahana Royal Patroness gently places a small clay seal or token into a monk’s open hands, her face calm but resolute, while attendants hold rolled documents behind her.

dialogue.text: The language of these records is clear. The property is hers to give. Land and revenue flow from her name into religious networks, and the law—whatever its exact form—recognizes her capacity.

i18n.hi: इन अभिलेखों की भाषा साफ है: संपत्ति उसकी है देने को। ज़मीन और लगान उसके नाम से धर्म–जाल में बहते हैं, और कानून – चाहे जैसा हो – उसकी क्षमता मानता है।

panels.shot: medium shot of a woman merchant and a nun standing together in a cave verandah
panels.action: A woman in trader’s attire stands beside a shaven-headed nun on a cave verandah, both looking outward over a busy trade route, while a young scribe kneels to note their donation.

dialogue.text: Nor are royal women alone. In the same scripts, nuns and merchant wives appear as donors. The world of names and gifts is not confined to the palace.

i18n.hi: औरतों में सिर्फ रानियाँ नहीं। उन्हीं लिपियों में भिक्षुणियाँ, व्यापारी–पत्नियाँ भी दानदाता हैं। नाम और दान की दुनिया सिर्फ महल तक सीमित नहीं।

panels.shot: extreme close-up on patroness’s thoughtful eyes as torchlight flickers
panels.action: By the flicker of lamplight inside a cave hall, Satavahana Royal Patroness’s eyes reflect the flames, her brow slightly knit in thought, the carved ceiling looming above.

dialogue.speaker: satavahana_royal_women
dialogue.text: If his name carries me, my kin must never doubt his throne.

i18n.hi: अगर उसका नाम मुझे संभाले, तो मेरे लोग कभी उसके राज पर शक न करें।

panels.shot: diagrammatic-style wide of inscriptions in different scripts and regions
panels.action: Multiple stone surfaces appear side by side: inscriptions from Nashik, Karla and Kanheri, their Brahmi letters varying slightly in style, suggesting spread across time and terrain.

dialogue.text: Scholars reading these scattered stones see a pattern. Matronymic names cluster within the Satavahana house, not across all society. They signal marriage politics, not a wholesale matrilineal order.

i18n.hi: इन बिखरे पत्थरों को पढ़ते विद्वान एक पैटर्न देखते हैं: मातृनाम ज़्यादातर सातवाहन घराने में सिमटे हैं, पूरी समाज में नहीं। वे विवाह–राजनीति दिखाते हैं, पूरा मातृवंश नहीं।

panels.shot: medium shot of a modern scholar in a library examining estampages
panels.action: A modern historian sits amid books and estampages of inscriptions, tracing Brahmi letters with a pencil, windows behind opening to imagined silhouettes of caves.

dialogue.text: Without a surviving Satavahana law code, the rest is careful inference. Epigraphy, language and comparison help reconstruct the legal space in which these women acted.

i18n.hi: सातवाहन का विधि–संहिता नहीं बची, तो बाकी सब सावधान अंदाज़ा है। शिलालेख, भाषा और तुलना मिलकर वही कानूनी जगह गढ़ते हैं, जिसमें ये औरतें चलती थीं।

panels.shot: wide shot of patroness walking away from a completed cave at dusk
panels.action: At dusk, Satavahana Royal Patroness walks down the rocky path from a completed cave façade, the carved pillars now still behind her, while monks and travelers begin to climb up.

dialogue.text: When the last chisel falls silent, the cave remains. Generations forget her face, but not her name. It survives as a matronymic, wrapped around her son’s royal claims.

i18n.hi: जब आखिरी छैनी थम जाती है, गुफा रह जाती है। पीढ़ियाँ उसका चेहरा भूलती हैं, नाम नहीं। वही नाम बेटे के राज–दावे पर लिपटे मातृनाम की तरह टिकता है।

panels.shot: slow pull-back from patroness’s name carved beside a king’s name
panels.action: The camera draws back from a close view of a king’s matronymic title where his mother’s name and his own run together along the basalt surface under layers of age-darkened patina.

dialogue.text: This is the quiet revolution of the Satavahana women: not overthrowing men, but inscribing themselves into the very names of kings, so that every royal title must also whisper a mother’s lineage.

i18n.hi: यही सातवाहन स्त्रियों की धीमी क्रांति है: पुरुषों को हटाना नहीं, खुद को राजाओं के नाम में उकेर देना, ताकि हर उपाधि में माँ के कुल की फुसफुसाहट रहे।

title_i18n.en: Son of Gautami, Son of Vasishthi

subtitle_i18n.en: Mothers, Names and Power in the Satavahana Deccan
subtitle_i18n.hi: माएँ, नाम और शक्ति – सातवाहन दक्कन
